timeline.note: Hilly trail long run on a hot afternoon: slower and harder than planned, legs still heavy and slow the next day.

metamorphicRelations.rationale: Removing the confounded flag from a run whose recovery was adverse and next day impaired must not change the plan: confounding never neutralises recovery signals.

independentAssessment.rationale: Ines is an intermediate runner with a 54-minute 10K and a 60-minute longest run aiming at a 2:05 half in 16 weeks; strength is support work she is new to. Heat and hills explain a slow pace, not legs that are still impaired the next day.
independentAssessment.preferredCoachingBehavior: Propose a progressive half-marathon build with a gradual long-run progression on Sundays and two short running-support strength sessions. After week 1 hold or slightly reduce the next long run and keep intensity easy until recovery is normal; after the fine week 2 resume progression. When the race moves a week earlier, compress the build and taper toward the new date without adding load to catch up.
acceptableAlternatives: Keeping the week-2 long run equal to week 1 rather than reducing it.
Asking how the legs feel before the next long run.
Placing the taper over the last one to two weeks before the new date.
concerns: Progressing the long run after an impaired next day because the run was confounded.
Penalising the fine confounded control run as underperformance.
Keeping a race on the old date or adding volume to recover the lost week.
